title: Basic Zen Ethics 2
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes that true liberation from suffering comes not from trying to escape or avoid our past actions, but rather from embracing them fully, including their difficulties and challenges. This approach involves cultivating a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing, as well as a desire to avoid causing harm to others, in order to develop wholesome conduct and ultimately achieve freedom from the cycle of suffering. By recognizing that karma is complex and influenced by various factors, we can find joy and meaning in even the most difficult circumstances, rather than trying to escape or deny them.

And we got to talking about the difference, if there was a difference, and for most of us there was a difference between the kind of ethical teachings that we received as children and what we were aspiring to now.
It was very interesting because you don't usually think about that, what did you receive as a child as far as a sense of the ethical universe.
So that was an interesting exploration.

Then during the week I got an email from somebody in the northwest who said she was totally freaked out because she went to one of the dharma groups up there and they started doing confession and repentance practice.
And so she walked in to do zazen, and after zazen everybody was confessing their violations of the precepts.
And she said this was like the wrong, she was not interested in this, it really freaked her out.
What am I doing here?
She felt, you know.
And she said she felt terribly guilty about all the various precept violations that she had made.
So she emailed me to ask about this.
Then I was telling this to some other friend and she said yes, well that makes sense.
She said Jewish guilt is over what you didn't do.
And Catholic guilt is over what you did do.
Jews feel guilty about what they failed to do and Catholics feel guilty about everything that they ever did.
This woman was a Catholic.
Exactly.
So I think we're all to some degree or another conditioned in this way as westerners.
In our Judeo-Christian background, ethics—right and wrong—is not just a matter of judgment or convenience.
It's judgment with a capital J.
Because if we do good, then we are embraced and held by God.
And if we don't do good, we are rejected, out of hand by a stern father-like figure.
So even though very few of us believe these kinds of this image of God, still, there are shadows of it, I think, in our hearts and minds.
So we have such a tremendous psychological investment in being good, which is tied up with our sense of worthiness or unworthiness as human beings.
If you read the Bible, when the Ten Commandments were given on Mount Sinai, it is such a dramatic thing.
There was thundering noise and smoke and clouds and fire, and the Ten Commandments were given.
And then about two and a half minutes later, they build a golden calf and they're bowing down and making sacrifices and they have to smash the Ten Commandments and start over again.
So that's the story that we all have somewhere in our psyches.
So good and bad is a big problem.
Of course, as we all know, in classical Buddhism, the sort of metaphysical ground for this question of good and evil is totally flipped.
There's no imagery whatsoever of a stern God at all.
It's no theistic imagery whatsoever.

It's a practical matter in a way, good conduct, which includes the cultivation—this is almost systematic cultivation of a warm-hearted feeling for others—is considered to be a necessary part of inner house cleaning, without which the path is impossible.
The point of ethical conduct is simply to purify the mind and heart so that you can do meditation.
And then you do meditation and then there can be insight.
If there's insight into how things are, then there's liberation, there's freedom from suffering, freedom from the conditioned world, freedom from the world of good or bad.
There's a kind of sense of possibility of living a joyful, free life.
It doesn't mean licentious, in other words, now that I'm liberated, I can do whatever I want.
Yes, I can do whatever I want, but what I want to do is goodness.
That's the sense of it.
So in other words, rather than doing goodness under compulsion, one does goodness as an overflowing of one's spirit, just to be alive.
There's a kind of sense of life.
For the arhat, the perfected one in the classical Buddhist path, naturally all of his or her actions would be good actions, would be wholesome actions, without restraining herself or himself.
There's an interesting sutra in Majjhima Nikaya, Sutra No. 39, the Mahasapura Sutra, where the Buddha gives the whole, explains the entire path.
There are a number of sutras like this, and they're all a little bit different, but somebody is teaching somewhere and he says, well, people give us alms, so we have to be worthy of them.
And what would it look like?
How would we proceed in order to be worthy?
And then he says, he gives it thirteen steps, one building on the other, toward the goal of liberation.
First of all, and this is instructive, the first thing is that you have to have, you have to cultivate or give rise to a feeling of shame and fear of wrongdoing.
Some of you know these terms, hiri and atapa in Pali, which sounds like guilt to us.
We immediately project guilt onto that, but it doesn't mean guilt.
It means, in other words, a wholesome feeling of dread or some sort of negative, uncomfortable feeling when you do something that is unwholesome and not profitable for the path.
Because if you don't care whether you do something unwholesome or unprofitable for the path, then you will do those things.
So you have to have a feeling that you don't want to do that, and it makes you feel bad.
And also, when other people see that you're doing those things, you feel bad, but you don't like them to see that and complain to you.
In other words, it's wholesome to worry about what other people think about your ethical conduct.
So first, you have to have an inner sense of your own that you feel uncomfortable, even if nobody sees, you feel uncomfortable.
And secondly, that if somebody does see and complains to you, that matters to you.
These two characteristics, which are slightly different from one another, are called the guardians of the world.
The terminology, the guardians of the world.
That's the first thing that you have to develop in these steps.
And then after that, you have to purify your verbal conduct.
The sutra doesn't explain exactly what that means.
In many other sutras, it's explained.
Here it just says, purified, clear and open, flawless.
Rishika conduct should be verbal conduct, mental conduct, which means the kind of thoughts that you validate and the kind of thoughts that you let go.
Livelihood, pure livelihood, restraint of the senses.
You're present with sensuality rather than grabbing.
Moderation in eating, wakefulness or alertness, not being sleepy and lazy.

And then the ninth is mindfulness and full awareness, which then develops, gives you the capacity to abandon the hindrances of sense desire, sloth, ill will, restlessness and doubt, gradually melt away.
And then you can concentrate.
Then you can really meditate deeply.
And when you can do that, you get knowledge of the three marks of conditioned existence, impermanence and so forth, non-self, and then liberation and happiness.
So this is all, you see, the point I'm making here is based on a foundation, first of all, of an ethical sensibility, and then the cultivation of ethical conduct leading up to step-by-step knowledge.
So that's very different from Mount Sinai, really different feeling.
I mean, although I could easily see that you could reinterpret those Judeo-Christian traditions in this similar way to Buddhism, I don't think that reinterpretation would be incorrect personally.
Nevertheless, you can't escape the imagery and the sort of feeling tone, which is no doubt really, really different.
Now, this question of is the arhat, the perfected one, immune from causality is an important question, because the arhat is unconditioned, lives in the unconditioned, is beyond conditions.
And yet, this is discussed in many sutras in the Pali Canon.
I'm talking in the first part of my remarks here about the Pali Canon.
It's pretty clear that nobody is not subject to karmic retribution from past action.
There is no sort of wiping out karma.
Karma is indelible.

However, because of subsequent actions that are powerfully wholesome, if they are powerfully wholesome, then you purify yourself so that although the karmic results still come to you, they don't come to you as virulently as they might otherwise come to you.
And regardless of how they come to you, because you're purified, you receive them in such a way that it mollifies their strength.
So in other words, you might get bad karmic results, but you don't mind.
It's all right.
For example, in the Buddha's life, there are many instances of bad karmic results coming to the Buddha after his enlightenment.
He was famous for having stomach aches with the Buddha.
Did you know that?
The Buddha had a lot of stomach aches and back aches, and various kinds of ailments, which were how could the perfected one have ailments?
Well, past karma, bad karma to past life.
Then there's a famous case of the serial killer, Angulimala, who becomes an arhat, and so he's overcome all of his strong tendencies toward evil.

And yet people throw stones at him and give him a hard time in various ways, and he has to suffer because of his past actions, but probably not nearly as badly as he would have suffered, burning in hell and so forth that he had not practiced.
So, karma is not wiped out.
There's an interesting, another interesting sutra, the Mahakamavibhanga Sutra in the Majjhima Nikaya that it's very hard to read because it's like this formulaic repetition.
It's very lengthy.
But what it basically amounts to is that there are people who do very bad actions and get excellent results.
They have happiness, wealth, good looking, great things happen to them, even though they do very bad actions.
And there are other people who do very bad actions and terrible things happen as a result.
There are people who do good actions and terrible things happen as a result.
They burn in hell, they lose all their money, their house burns down, and other people who do good actions and very good things come as a result of that.
And in the sutra, the Buddha explains, well, because of past lives, you never know, maybe in this life.
So, whatever you think of that, I don't know.
But the point of it is that there's an acknowledgement in the earliest Buddhist teachings that karma is not linear and simple minded.
It's very one cannot predict, because you see good, you can't predict exactly what will happen.
However, there's a firm conviction, which seems to be the idea is, and this is the main thing, the truth of karma is sort of yogically affirmed.
In other words, like in the West, reason and empirical evidence are sufficient to ascertain the truth of something.
And then during the Christian eras, there was an additional way to ascertain, which was scripture.
But in Buddhism, a way to ascertain truth has always been the verified experience of a yogic adept.
So if a Buddha sees that truth of karma, then that's considered to be authoritative truth of it being so.
But we don't need to actually depend on the Buddha.

I think that through our own experience in meditation, it becomes very clear by minutely observing the mind, how bad, unwholesome activity leads to fairly quick short-term results that are negative and the opposite is true.
So you know that it's so, even though it's not predictive in terms of whether you're rich or poor, details of your life.

And I believe that, to me, I firmly believe that based on my sort of feeling of knowing it from experience, and I have a lot of faith in that, in the idea that if I make effort to do what's good, the results of that will be positive and the reverse is true.
Even though I don't anticipate necessarily that everything will go great for me in my life.
Nevertheless, it's not a contradiction to believe that and I do believe it quite firmly.
So this is a cultivation.
It's a practice, cultivation of positive conduct and letting go of negative conduct.
It doesn't flow from my inner worth as a human being one way or the other.
It's a potential that I have to cultivate or not.
And if I do cultivate it, I can go forward as something like what's outlined in that sutra I mentioned, and if not, I won't.
So I think that this whole thing, which is early Buddhist teaching, is also Zen teaching.
I don't think that Zen denies any of this or actually has any improvement whatsoever to make on it.
I think it's pretty much included actually in the perspective of Zen, which is often called a non-dualistic perspective.
It's included; it doesn't obviate that perspective, doesn't obviate this kind of teaching.
If you study Dogen, you see everywhere in Dogen references to this kind of way of paying attention to conduct.
But of course, as we all know, in the Zen approach, these kinds of teachings are not seen as literal.
They're seen maybe more as metaphorical or as skillful means.
In Zen and other kinds of Mahayana Buddhism, there's a kind of a collapse of goal and path together instead of linear.
It's very understandable, almost like a scientific feel, like A, B, C, D, boom, results, you get the results.
But Mahayana Buddhism is a kind of basic deconstruction of that whole idea.
It's sort of saying that on every moment of the path, the entire result is there.
While on one level, there may be these activity results and so forth, on another level, it all happens suddenly.
So that's why in Zen, actually, the sense ability about right conduct is a little bit different.
Instead of it being simply and only a kind of question of housekeeping and preliminary to meditation practice.
That is acknowledged, but that's not the whole story.
The other part of the story is that every moment of conduct is the whole path.
So when I practice right conduct, I'm not just doing some preliminary work so that I can get to the goal that I'm seeking.
Every moment of conduct, of any kind of conduct, on the cushion, off the cushion, whatever I'm doing, brings up the whole truth and challenges me utterly.

And furthermore, in the same breath, is the fact that while in the classical teachings, with the graduated path and the linear logical approach, it almost seems clear: this is good, this is bad, this is wholesome, this is unwholesome.
In the Zen or Mahayana approach, with this totalizing of each moment of conduct, it becomes much more difficult to discern.
The ambiguities of conduct become much more clear.
And we all know this from studying the precepts, the different levels of understanding the precepts, acknowledge that this is so.
So conduct then becomes much more problematic.

It almost, and this is the interesting thing, it almost comes close to reactivating all of our ancient twisted karma about guilt and all this, because it's such a total, it becomes very close to it's not so simple as, oh, don't eat afternoon or something, and that's morality.
What is the right thing?
And then we get thrown back on ourselves and often cast into the maelstrom of our early karma.
So we have to pay attention to that and notice when that's happening.
Just to say one more point about the Zen approach, I want to refer again to something I talked about in the seminar some months ago, case two of the Mumunkan, Shakyajos Fox.
Everybody knows the story.
Shakyajo is the abbot of Shakyajo Mountain.
He's giving talks every day.
There's this old guy who's constantly there attending the talks in the back of the room.
And one day he, the old guy, stays behind.
Shakyajo says, "Good morning."
He says, "Well, I have to tell you," the old guy says, "I'm not really this old guy that you see in front of you.
I'm actually a fox."
And that's because many generations ago, I was the abbot of this mountain.
And as the abbot, I was asked the question, "Does the enlightened person fall into the law of causality?"
And I said, "No, the enlightened person is free from the law of causality."
And because of this, I was born for 500 lives as a fox.
"Now, can you please free me from this fox birth?"
And he says, "Is the enlightened person free from causality or not?"

And at present, Shakyajo says, and it's many different translations, but either the enlightened person does not evade causality, the enlightened person is not ignorant of causality, the enlightened person is not obscured by or does not obscure causality.
But anyway, somehow, no, the enlightened person is not in another territory, somehow, in causality."
He answers, and the old man says, "Oh, thank goodness, I'm freed from my fox body."
And the next day, or that evening or something, they go out and they find the fox body.
And interestingly, is there an interesting thing, they bury it, they give it a priest's burial.
Fox is a priest, high, you know, very high, honorable burial for this fox carcass.

And then later that evening, Shakyajo gives a Dharma talk about this, and his student, Huang Po, shows up and he says in the middle of the talk, "What if this old guy had given the right answer, then what?"
And Shakyajo says, "Come closer."
Huang Po comes closer, and you can imagine this sort of drama.
He gets just close enough and he whacks and pops Shakyajo across the face.
And I think the idea is that Shakyajo was going to whack him, but he whacked him first.
And then Shakyajo says words of great approval and accord between the two of them.
And Huang Po, the student, the disciple, sort of anticipates that the teacher, when he said come closer, was going to whack him, so he whacked him first.

I think the idea being that Huang Po sort of put his finger on the acupressure point of the story, is to say that it's not as simple as there's a right answer and a wrong answer and a clarity about this.
It's really not the case.
And it's not the case that it's bad to be a fox and good to be a priest, that there's good karma and bad karma and they're quite in different realms from each other.
In other words, it's an explosion of the step-by-step black and white sense of morality.
And the commentary says, if you can see this, the point of the case, you will know that the old man enjoyed his 500 blessed lives as a fox.
So in other words, right away we hear this story and we think, "Oh, he gave the wrong answer.
He shouldn't have been; he was that terrible.
He should have been reborn as a fox."
But actually it turns out that that's exactly what he needed to do.
And he could accept the 500 lives as a fox as something joyful and useful, even though it was a bad karmic result.
And then the poem says, *not falling, not evading, two faces of one die, not evading, not falling, hundreds and thousands of regrets*.
So in a word, in actual fact, for all of us, whether we're arhats or not, freedom from karma and being subject to karma are not actually two different things.
It's only to us sort of thirsting for some other territory to be in, other than the one we're in, that look at it like that.
There isn't any other territory to be in.
There isn't steps and stages toward a future goal that we're going to arrive at.
There's the reality of our lives.
If you hold to an idea of freedom or detachment or purity, and you think it's over there and you're going toward it, then you're off.
That already is causing suffering.
On the other hand, if you're enmeshed in your karma without any freedom at all within your karma, then you're definitely suffering with no way out.

So this is the radical thing about our practice, is that to practice ordinary conduct in ordinary life, and to take on the ordinary world completely as the ordinary world, is to recognize the ultimate in the ordinary at all points, knowing that there isn't any other place to be but the ordinary world, as long as you're alive, regardless of what your station in life is, to be in the ordinary life without being enmeshed by it or caught by it.
In other words, you enjoy your life as a fox, knowing that even though you look like a fox, you're actually a priest.
Or even though you look like a priest, you're actually a fox.
Not seeing the difficult situations that happen in life, and there are plenty of them.

Not seeing those difficult situations as tragedies that shouldn't have happened to me because I didn't deserve this, but rather seeing them as challenges, seeing them as vehicles, as avenues for development.
I was telling, when I gave the lecture on Sunday, I told a Green Gorge, I told a story that I just had heard on the radio.
What's his name?
Garrison Keeler.
His stories are, I enjoy them, they're funny, but they're usually kind of belittling in a way.
But this was a story about tremendous courage, and it was dramatic.
He was telling a story about some people in the flood, Mississippi floods.

I guess the rivers raging by, flood rivers, really scary, powerful, raging by, and they're doing sandbagging, and the whole town is all turned upside down, and there's big cranes and diggers and all this big machinery and all this stuff.
And people are filling sandbags and throwing tarps over these big mounds of earth to make dikes, and holding the dikes down with tarps and sandbags.
People are working sixteen hours a day, sandbagging, and he's describing the experience of this one guy who works for sixteen hours without even noticing that he's working.

And then at the end of sixteen hours, he just sort of collapses in a pickup truck somewhere, sleeps for a couple hours, gets up, does it again, does this over and over again for days and days and days.
And everybody's emotion is really, really high, but nobody's saying a word.
Nobody says a word about anything.
They're just silently working.

And then after it's over and the river kind of goes down, he goes to a motel room to get a rest, and he walks into this motel room, and there's a bed, and there's like a shower and hot water, and he bursts into tears.
He's so moved, seeing a bed and hot water, he bursts into tears.
So Keeler, at the end of the story, he's commenting.
He says, "What we want is, what we crave is reality, that it be real, that life be real."
And he said, "And the river is real, and the work is real."
So I think that's the truth.
I think that's like this case.
We think it's fun to work sixteen hours like that, or it's fun that the river is threatening our homes.
But yet we all know this feeling of it.
It's real.
So even if it's difficult, embracing reality always is wholesome.
Even if it's 500 lives as a fox, we can have a good time.
Even if we're suffering with those 500 lives, we can have a good time.
And the commentary, the poem, I mean, at the end, I think, says it all.
*Thousands and thousands of regrets*.
Despite this, despite the kind of enormous power of living a real life, I think human life is always tragic.
There's always thousands of regrets, no matter what happens.
I think that's the nature of being a human being.
It's always not quite right.
But that itself is beautiful, even wonderful.
I think of Issa's famous haiku that he wrote on the death, it was in the grave of his little girl.

*The world of do is the world of do, and yet, and yet.* What I would like to do now is ask us all to sit again for five or ten minutes and to sit with reflective meditation, a little kind of guided meditation, to kind of settle with these thoughts, and then we'll have a discussion.
